analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks and credit unions under $50 billion in assets from direct consumer-watchdog examinations.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the consumer bureau's oversight threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion died in committee without ever getting a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) directly examines banks and credit unions with $10 billion or more in assets to make sure they follow consumer protection laws. This bill would have raised that cutoff to $50 billion, removing hundreds of mid-sized banks and credit unions from the bureau's direct oversight. The bill was introduced in the House, referred to the Financial Services Committee, and never advanced before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions with assets between $10 billion and $50 billion would gain directly: they would no longer face regular CFPB examinations and would no longer file the bureau's detailed reports. Regulators estimate this covers roughly 150 to 200 institutions. These firms would save compliance costs, and their consumer-law compliance would be checked only by their own primary regulators instead of the dedicated consumer watchdog. The bill's sponsor was a Democrat, and its three cosponsors were Republicans.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold at which insured banks and credit unions come under the CFPB's direct supervisory purview from $10 billion to $50 billion, freeing firms in between from the bureau's exams [S2][S3].
Raises the reporting threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion as well, so firms under $50 billion would no longer be subject to the bureau's reporting requirements [S2][S3].
The change would take effect 45 days after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, consumers banking at mid-sized institutions would bear the risk: the CFPB would no longer directly examine those firms for consumer-law violations such as illegal fees, deceptive marketing, or discriminatory lending. That oversight burden would shift to the banks' other regulators, which share supervisory duties with the institutions they oversee. Any savings banks gained from reduced compliance could be kept as profit or passed to shareholders rather than necessarily to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers at mid-sized banks and credit unions

drawbacks.text: The bill removes direct CFPB examinations for banks and credit unions holding between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets, leaving consumer-law enforcement at those firms to regulators that also supervise the same institutions' safety and soundness — a structural conflict the CFPB was created in 2010 to break [S2][S3].

The $50 billion cutoff is a sharp jump, roughly five times the current threshold, so a large group of institutions would exit direct federal consumer oversight at once rather than the smallest firms being carved out [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that the $10 billion line captures institutions small enough that direct CFPB supervision adds cost without much added protection, and that exam and reporting requirements are expensive for mid-sized firms. The counterargument is that the bill's savings flow to the banks while the risk — weaker detection of consumer abuses at hundreds of institutions — falls on their customers. Because the bill died in committee, neither change ever took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee after being referred there the day it was introduced, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the bill in the House on November 19, 2015, joined by Rep. Steve Stivers [S1][S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which was the only committee action it ever received [S1][S5].
Three House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, leaving the bill to die in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mid-sized banks and credit unions did not get the exemption they sought, so the CFPB's direct examination and reporting authority over institutions above $10 billion remained in place — the outcome consumers' advocates wanted and the bill's banking-industry beneficiaries did not achieve.

for.name: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the CFPB's examination and reporting thresholds from $10 billion to $50 billion.

for.name: 3 of 246 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Steve Stivers, who joined at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and only three Republican cosponsors, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan divide on the merits appears in the record.

industries.industry: Mid-sized banks and credit unions ($10–$50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would have removed them from direct CFPB examinations and reporting, cutting their compliance costs while shifting the risk of undetected consumer-law violations onto their own customers.
The bureau would lose direct supervisory jurisdiction over all institutions below $50 billion in assets, shrinking the reach of the consumer watchdog Congress created in 2010.
